name: Seswaa
subtitle: Beef boiled until it falls apart and pounded, cooked by men for weddings and funerals.

facts.label: Pot
facts.value: three-legged iron pot, or large iron pots on wood fires

facts.label: Served with
facts.value: bogobe (sorghum porridge) and madila (fermented milk), or samp and beans

parts.text: Seswaa is a salty pounded meat dish prepared by men, simmered until soft with salt, cooking oil and water in a three-legged iron pot, a student writes.
It is a standard delicacy at most traditional events, including weddings and funerals.
A safari company calls it Botswana's national dish and says beef is boiled slowly with little more than water and salt.
Large iron pots simmer over wood fires for hours; when the meat is tender it is lifted into large carved wooden mortars and pounded with heavy pestles until the fibres separate.

The two sources differ on details: one lists cooking oil among the ingredients and speaks of the dish as prepared by men; the other says several people work together, with elders supervising by experience rather than by the clock.
Meals pair a protein with a starch and a relish. Starches the student lists include sorghum mixed with yellow melon and sour milk, samp with beans, and flat breads.
The safari company says seswaa is served with bogobe, a sorghum porridge, and madila, fermented milk.

The safari company writes that nothing about seswaa is individual: it is prepared collectively, served generously and eaten together, and offering it to guests means welcoming them into the community.

gaps: Where the dish comes from and how old it is. Neither source gives a history, and the safari company's article does not cite any.
The voice of Batswana cooks. The sources are a visiting student and a travel company writing for outsiders.
The name seswaa and its variants in different parts of Botswana and South Africa: not covered by the sources read.
Quantities and cuts of meat: not given.
Where to eat it, and what it costs.
The photograph shows a plate with samp, beans and seswaa; where it was taken is not stated.
